claim: Zebrafish ZP2 isoforms present 31.09–33.09% identity to mouse ZP2.
source: Zebrafish ZP2 isoforms present 31.09–33.09% identity to mouse ZP2 (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data presented in Figure 1A, which shows the comparison between zebrafish and mouse ZP2 proteins.

claim: The first 6-cysteine residues of zebrafish ZP2 are organized into a trefoil domain.
source: The first 6-cysteine residues of zebrafish ZP2 are organized into a trefoil domain, and zebrafish ZP2 lacks the homologous domain to the mammalian N-terminal region (Figure 1A), which has been reported to be necessary and sufficient to support mouse and human sperm binding (Avella et al., 2014; Tokuhiro and Dean, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 1A and references to published literature.

claim: Zebrafish ZP2 lacks the homologous domain to the mammalian N-terminal region.
source: The first 6-cysteine residues of zebrafish ZP2 are organized into a trefoil domain, and zebrafish ZP2 lacks the homologous domain to the mammalian N-terminal region (Figure 1A), which has been reported to be necessary and sufficient to support mouse and human sperm binding (Avella et al., 2014; Tokuhiro and Dean, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data in Figure 1A showing the absence of the N-terminal domain.

claim: The mammalian ZP2 N-terminal region has been reported to be necessary and sufficient to support mouse and human sperm binding.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: Mouse sperm bound sparsely to beads coated with either zebrafish ZP2 or ZP3.
source: Confocal images and quantification with boxplots showed that mouse sperm bound sparsely to beads coated with either zebrafish ZP2 or ZP3 and to beads coated with both zebrafish ZP2 and ZP3, yet bound efficiently to beads coated with mouse ZP2 (Figure 1C and D; Avella et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy images and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Mouse sperm bound sparsely to beads coated with both zebrafish ZP2 and ZP3.
source: Confocal images and quantification with boxplots showed that mouse sperm bound sparsely to beads coated with either zebrafish ZP2 or ZP3 and to beads coated with both zebrafish ZP2 and ZP3, yet bound efficiently to beads coated with mouse ZP2 (Figure 1C and D; Avella et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy images and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Mouse sperm bound efficiently to beads coated with mouse ZP2.
source: Confocal images and quantification with boxplots showed that mouse sperm bound sparsely to beads coated with either zebrafish ZP2 or ZP3 and to beads coated with both zebrafish ZP2 and ZP3, yet bound efficiently to beads coated with mouse ZP2 (Figure 1C and D; Avella et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy images and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Beads coated with individual zebrafish ZP2 or ZP3, or with both ZP2 and ZP3, cannot support sperm binding in vitro as efficiently as mouse ZP2.
source: Therefore, we could conclude that beads coated with individual zebrafish ZP2 or ZP3, or with both ZP2 and ZP3, cannot support sperm binding in vitro as efficiently as mouse ZP2 (Figure 1D).

claim: Zebrafish oocytes presented no signs of zona deterioration within the first 60 min under mouse IVF conditions.

claim: The isolated chorion was found to not support mouse sperm binding.

claim: Mouse sperm bind to the fish chorion (0.025±0.11, s.e.m.) with significantly lower efficiency to mouse zonae (0.76±0.05, s.e.m.).

(Figure 1F, top-right), and with comparable efficiency to the zonae surrounding mouse two-cell embryos (0.041±0.01, s.e.m.) (Figure 1F, bottom-right).

claim: Mouse sperm bind to the fish chorion with comparable efficiency to the zonae surrounding mouse two-cell embryos (0.041±0.01, s.e.m.).

(Figure 1F, top-right), and with comparable efficiency to the zonae surrounding mouse two-cell embryos (0.041±0.01, s.e.m.) (Figure 1F, bottom-right).

claim: Mouse sperm bind to the chorion surrounding zebrafish eggs with comparable efficiency (0.06±0.02 s.e.m.) as to the chorion only (no oocyte within) isolated from zebrafish eggs in Hank's solution.

claim: Mouse sperm cannot bind to the zebrafish chorion.
source: From these observations, we conclude that mouse sperm cannot bind to the zebrafish chorion.

claim: No zebrafish sperm bound to the mouse zona pellucida.

claim: Zebrafish sperm do not interact with mouse zonae.
source: These results support the hypothesis that zebrafish sperm do not interact with mouse zonae.

claim: The micropyle region of ovulated oocytes is known to attract fish sperm.
source: Although the chorion does not support mouse sperm binding, the micropyle region of ovulated oocytes is known to attract fish sperm (Yanagimachi, 1957; Yanagimachi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: The micropyle attraction is due to the presence of still unidentified glycosylated protein(s) present in the micropylar region of fish eggs.
source: This is due to the presence of still unidentified glycosylated protein(s) present in the micropylar region of fish eggs (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by WGA staining shown in Figure 2A and B, which detects glycoproteins.

claim: Yanagimachi et al., 2017, reported the absence of detectable glycoproteins in the micropyle.
source: Yanagimachi et al., 2017, reported the absence of detectable glycoproteins in the micropyle, whereas Dingare et al., 2018, identified glycoprotein expression localized to the micropyle region.

claim: Dingare et al., 2018, identified glycoprotein expression localized to the micropyle region.

claim: Freshly ovulated zebrafish oocytes show a positive WGA-633 signal in the micropylar region.
source: We confirmed the presence of a positive signal in the micropylar region of zebrafish oocytes (Figure 2A), as previously described (Dingare et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 2A and citation to previous work.

claim: When the MP was biochemically removed with trypsin, the number of zebrafish sperm surrounding the micropylar region or entering the micropyle significantly decreased.
source: The presence of sperm after insemination was found to depend on the presence of the MP. Indeed, when the MP was biochemically removed with trypsin (Figure 2C and D), the number of zebrafish sperm surrounding the micropylar region or entering the micropyle significantly decreased (Figure 2E and F), which also led to a reduction in the fertilization rates (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2C-F comparing trypsin-treated and untreated eggs.

claim: Removal of the MP led to a reduction in the fertilization rates.
source: The presence of sperm after insemination was found to depend on the presence of the MP. Indeed, when the MP was biochemically removed with trypsin (Figure 2C and D), the number of zebrafish sperm surrounding the micropylar region or entering the micropyle significantly decreased (Figure 2E and F), which also led to a reduction in the fertilization rates (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by fertilization rate data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Mouse sperm accumulate to the chorion area surrounding the micropyle upon in vitro insemination of zebrafish ovulated oocytes.
source: While performing our cross-species insemination assay, upon in vitro insemination of zebrafish ovulated oocytes with mouse sperm (37°C, 5% CO2, HTF/HSA), we could observe the accumulation of mouse sperm to the chorion area surrounding the micropyle (Figure 3A, left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The binding of mouse sperm to the micropyle region persisted after extensive washes with a glass pipette.
source: This binding persisted after extensive washes with a glass pipette, which was able to detach loosely bound mouse sperm to mouse two-cell embryos (negative control; Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations comparing binding stability to negative controls.

claim: The micropylar region of the isolated chorion supported mouse sperm binding.
source: Then, to assess the ability of the zebrafish micropyle to support mouse sperm binding independently from the oocyte, we mechanically isolated the chorion in Hank's solution to prevent oocyte activation. The micropylar region of the isolated chorion supported mouse sperm binding (Figure 3A, right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mouse sperm bound the micropylar region (1.11±0.1, s.e.m.) with comparable efficiency to mouse zonae pellucidae (1.07±0.07, s.e.m.) surrounding ovulated eggs.
source: Upon quantification of these observations with boxplots, we found that mouse sperm bound the micropylar region (1.11±0.1, s.e.m.) with comparable efficiency to mouse zonae pellucidae (1.07±0.07, s.e.m.) surrounding ovulated eggs (Figure 3B), while sperm bound to the chorion away from the micropyle (at a radial distance greater than 160 µm from the opening of the micropyle) were rarely observed (0.2±0.04, s.e.m.).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Sperm bound to the chorion away from the micropyle (at a radial distance greater than 160 µm from the opening of the micropyle) were rarely observed (0.2±0.04, s.e.m.).
source: Upon quantification of these observations with boxplots, we found that mouse sperm bound the micropylar region (1.11±0.1, s.e.m.) with comparable efficiency to mouse zonae pellucidae (1.07±0.07, s.e.m.) surrounding ovulated eggs (Figure 3B), while sperm bound to the chorion away from the micropyle (at a radial distance greater than 160 µm from the opening of the micropyle) were rarely observed (0.2±0.04, s.e.m.).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Trypsin digestion of the chorion virtually eliminated the MP as shown by the absence of WGA-633 staining.
source: Trypsin digestion of the chorion virtually eliminated the MP as shown by the absence of WGA-633 staining (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Trypsin-treated micropyle regions did not support mouse sperm binding.
source: When inseminated with mouse sperm, trypsin-treated micropyle regions did not support sperm binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Mouse sperm can recognize the fish micropyle in vitro, and such recognition is dependent on the presence of the MP.
source: From these observations, we concluded that mouse sperm can recognize the fish micropyle in vitro, and such recognition is dependent on the presence of the MP.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing MP-dependent sperm binding.

claim: Fluorescence density increases from the periphery toward the central 40 µm area encompassing the micropyle region.
source: We found that fluorescence density increases from the periphery toward the central 40 µm area encompassing the micropyle region (Figure 3D, left-Y axis).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 3D.

claim: An increasing number of mouse sperm bound to the chorion from the periphery toward the micropyle.
source: Of note, we observed an increasing number of mouse sperm bound to the chorion from the periphery toward the micropyle (Figure 3D, right-Y axis).
evidence: The claim is supported by sperm count data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The direct correlation between the increasing fluorescence density and the number of sperm bound from the periphery toward the micropyle is consistent with the potential role of the MP as a chemoattractant to guide sperm toward the micropyle.
source: The direct correlation between the increasing fluorescence density and the number of sperm bound from the periphery toward the micropyle is consistent with the potential role of the MP as a chemoattractant to guide sperm toward the micropyle (Yanagimachi, 1957; Yanagimachi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the correlation observed in the data, supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Only a subpopulation of sperm was able to enter the micropyle canal (8.25±3.63, 5.92%±2.38%).
source: The results showed that only a subpopulation of sperm was able to enter the micropyle canal (8.25±3.63, 5.92%±2.38%), while the majority were found not entering the micropyle and either swimming close to the micropyle without entering (110.5±44.04, 79.20%±5.42%) or passing by and completely ignoring the zebrafish oocyte (17.75±4.22, 15.00%±6.28%)(quantification performed as displayed in Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: The majority of sperm were found not entering the micropyle and either swimming close to the micropyle without entering (110.5±44.04, 79.20%±5.42%) or passing by and completely ignoring the zebrafish oocyte (17.75±4.22, 15.00%±6.28%).

claim: Mouse sperm entered the micropyle canal within 24.5±7.1 s after approaching the zebrafish oocyte.

claim: Mouse sperm that crossed the micropyle represented 0.11587 ±0.0001% of the total inseminated progressively motile sperm.

claim: Mouse sperm were never observed to fuse with the zebrafish egg cell under experimental conditions.
source: Additionally, both acrosome-intact and acrosome-reacted sperm were found in the ICS via confocal microscopy and TEM (Figure 4F and G), though they were never observed to fuse with the egg cell under our experimental conditions (Figure 4D), possibly due to predicted low affinity between the Izumo1-Spaca6-Tmem81 mouse sperm trimeric complex (Deneke et al., 2024) with the zebrafish egg cell protein Bouncer.

claim: Based on AlphaFold2-Multimer structural predictions, low binding affinity was observed between zebrafish Bouncer and the mouse trimer (Izumo1+Spaca6+Tmem81) as indicated by low interface-predicted template modeling (ipTM) scores and high predicted aligned error (PAE) values.

claim: Mouse sperm can recognize the micropylar region of zebrafish oocytes and cross the micropyle inner opening regardless of the acrosome status.
